title: The lost sheep (Luke 15:3–7)
hookLine: a shepherd leaves ninety-nine in the open to go after one

cards: Ten friends in a group chat, jokes every night. Then one stops replying. No fight.
They just drift, and after a week the chat rolls on without them. Most of us have been on both sides of that. Now a shepherd at dusk, counting his flock in: ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine.
One short. It's getting dark, and any sensible person would call it a good day and shut the gate. He doesn't.
He leaves the ninety-nine in the open country and walks back out into the hills, after one.

teach.b: Luke says why Jesus told it.

People with bad reputations, tax collectors and others everyone called sinners, kept coming close to listen, and some of the religious teachers grumbled: "This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them."
Remember day ten: he ate with the wrong people on purpose.

This story is his answer, and it opens with a question: "What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?"
Until he find it. Not until it's too dark. And wilderness here means open grazing land, not a jungle.
The risk is real: the ninety-nine are left on their own. Then the part people forget. He doesn't scold the sheep or drag it home.

"He layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing." A grown sheep is heavy; he carries it anyway, happy. At home he calls his friends and neighbors: "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost."
Jesus ends plainly: more joy in heaven over one person who turns back than over ninety-nine who never needed to.
His listeners knew the old picture, the Psalm that begins "The Lord is my shepherd," and Christians have seen God in this shepherd ever since.
Some of the oldest Christian paintings, in the Roman catacombs, show a young shepherd with a sheep across his shoulders. As math, one in a hundred is terrible. But the story isn't doing math.
To God, nobody is a rounding error.

how: Christians often picture Jesus as the Good Shepherd, and this parable is read in churches as a picture of God searching for anyone who has wandered off. Many churches take its name for their outreach to people who have stopped coming.

p: leaves the ninety-nine, goes after one

s: the shepherd brings the sheep home and scolds it
"he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing." no scolding. a party.
Jesus told the story because people complained about who he ate with
"this man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." the story is his answer.
the wilderness here means a thick jungle
it means open grazing land. the ninety-nine are left out in the open.

games.q: you're a shepherd. it's getting dark, and you count ninety-nine. one sheep is missing out in the hills. what do you do?
o: shut the gate: ninety-nine is a good day.
leave the ninety-nine and go after the one.
wait till morning and look then.
games.why: he leaves the ninety-nine in the open and goes after the one "until he find it." then he carries it home, rejoicing.

practice: Scroll back, in your head, through the people who used to be around: a friend from school, a cousin, a coworker who moved on.

Let one face come up, someone who drifted, not someone who hurt you, and hold them in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wish them well, wherever they are tonight.

wordCard.voice: Wilderness. The word Luke uses for the open grazing land where the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to walk back out after the one.

orig.note: Greek: sheep. the word Luke uses for the one that wandered off.

carryVoice: Your line: one is worth the walk. Next, the search moves indoors, with a lamp and a broom.
